The cultural impact was enormous. Indigenous religious practices did not disappear but went underground or blended with Christianity to create syncretic forms of worship. The syncretism also reshaped the Americas culturally: Spanish language, Catholic religion, European agricultural practices and livestock (horses, cattle, pigs) all transformed indigenous societies within a generation.

Key Fact

Spanish missionaries destroyed most Aztec codices and demolished indigenous temples, building Christian churches on the same foundations. The Aztec Templo Mayor in Mexico City was demolished and its stones used to build the new Spanish cathedral.

The Columbian Exchange and European Impact

The conquest initiated the Columbian Exchange — a vast transfer of goods, crops, animals and diseases in both directions across the Atlantic. From the Americas to Europe came maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chilli peppers, cacao and tobacco. These crops transformed European and global diets. From Europe to the Americas came wheat, cattle, horses, sugar cane, diseases and enslaved Africans.

The most dramatic European economic consequence was the Price Revolution: a sustained period of inflation across Europe during the sixteenth century. Spanish silver from the Americas — particularly from Potosí — flooded into European circulation, increasing the money supply and driving up prices. Wages lagged behind prices, impoverishing workers and peasants. Historians debate how much of the Price Revolution was caused by American silver versus other factors, but the connection is well established. Spain itself was paradoxically weakened by its silver wealth: easy money reduced incentives for domestic industry, and by the late sixteenth century Spain was using silver to pay for imports rather than building its own manufacturing base.

The conquest opened new trade routes and created new commodities. Cacao (chocolate) was initially used as currency in the Aztec empire and was introduced to Europe in the sixteenth century; by the seventeenth century it had become a luxury drink across Europe. Tobacco, also from the Americas, transformed European social habits. Sugar, grown in the Caribbean with enslaved African labour (as indigenous populations collapsed), became one of the most profitable commodities of the early modern period. The Atlantic economy — linking Europe, Africa and the Americas in a triangular trade — was a direct consequence of the voyages that began with Columbus in 1492.

unit_name: Voyages of Discovery and Conquest of the Americas, 1492-1522
lesson_title: Interpretations: discovery, conquest or invasion?
content_html:
Why Interpretations of 1492 Differ

The events of 1492–1522 have been interpreted very differently across five centuries. An interpretation is not simply a description of what happened — it is a judgement about what those events meant, who was responsible and how they should be evaluated. Interpretations change because new evidence is found, because the societies writing history change, and because the questions historians ask change. The conquest of the Americas is one of the most contested events in world history precisely because so much was at stake: empire, religion, race, identity and memory.

For exam questions about why interpretations differ, you need to focus on the authors themselves: who they were, when they wrote, what evidence they used, and what purpose they had. The “what” (what each interpretation says) is easier but earns fewer marks than the “why” (why they differ).

Key Fact

Interpretations differ because of: the author’s identity and background; the purpose of the account (justification, criticism, commemoration); the evidence available to the author; and the time and context in which they wrote. All four factors matter for the 10-mark Compare Interpretations question.

Spanish Chronicles: Cortés and Bernal Díaz del Castillo

Bernal Díaz del Castillo was a soldier who participated in the conquest of Mexico and wrote his memoir, the Historia Verdadera (“True History of the Conquest of New Spain”), completed around 1568 — nearly fifty years after the events. His account is vivid and detailed, describing Tenochtitlán’s wonders and the brutality of combat with equal honesty. He is often praised as a more reliable witness than Cortés himself, because he had less to gain from distorting the record.

Cortés’s own Cartas de Relación (Letters of Account) were written to King Charles I to justify his unauthorised expedition and secure royal favour. They emphasise Spanish bravery, the justice of the conquest and the need to bring Christianity to the Americas. Cortés routinely minimised his own brutality, presented indigenous peoples as barbaric and his actions as necessary for civilisation and Christianity. These letters are invaluable as sources — but they are advocacy documents, not neutral history.

The Black Legend (Leyenda Negra) was a narrative used by Spain’s Protestant rivals — England, the Netherlands and France — to portray Spanish colonial rule as uniquely cruel and barbaric. It drew heavily on Bartolomé de las Casas’s Brief Account (1542), which had been widely translated and illustrated with graphic images of Spanish violence. The irony is that Las Casas wrote to reform Spain from within; his words were used externally to condemn Spain as a whole. Spanish defenders argued that the Black Legend was propaganda, pointing out that other European colonisers (English, Dutch, French) were equally violent and exploitative but were not held to the same standard. This debate — whether Spanish colonialism was uniquely brutal or simply characteristic of its era — continues among historians today.

Nahua and Indigenous Accounts

The most important indigenous-perspective source is the Florentine Codex, compiled by the Spanish friar Bernardino de Sahagún in the 1570s using interviews with elderly Nahua informants who remembered the conquest. Book 12 of the Florentine Codex contains the Nahua account of the conquest — one of the few surviving indigenous-perspective narratives. It describes the terror of the Spanish advance, the smell of gunpowder, the shock of horses and the devastation of the siege. The Nahua informants do not portray the conquest as a heroic liberation but as a catastrophe.

However, the Florentine Codex was compiled decades after the events, in Spanish colonial conditions, and mediated through Sahagún’s translation and editorial decisions. Historians debate how far the Nahua voices in the codex were shaped or distorted by the friar’s own agenda (he wanted to understand indigenous culture to convert it more effectively) and by the changed political context in which survivors were speaking. It is a crucial source — but its limitations must be acknowledged.

Key Fact

The Florentine Codex (1570s), compiled by Friar Sahagún with Nahua informants, is the main indigenous-perspective account of the conquest. Its limitations include: compiled fifty years after the events; in Spanish colonial conditions; translated and edited by a Spanish friar; informants may have shaped their testimony to suit the post-conquest environment.

Modern Historians: Hugh Thomas and Decolonial Perspectives

Hugh Thomas’s Conquest: Montezuma, Cortés and the Fall of Old Mexico (1993) became the most widely read modern account of the conquest. Thomas drew on a vast range of sources in Spanish, Nahuatl and other languages to present a nuanced picture of all the main actors. He is sometimes criticised by decolonial historians for emphasising individual agency (Cortés’s brilliance, Moctezuma’s miscalculations) in ways that can downplay the structural violence of colonialism and the scale of indigenous suffering.

From the late twentieth century, particularly around the 500th anniversary of 1492, a growing movement of decolonial historians and indigenous scholars challenged the framing of the voyages as “discovery.” They argued that the term “discovery” erases the millions of people who already lived in the Americas and frames the event from a European perspective. From an indigenous viewpoint, 1492 was not a discovery but an invasion, followed by genocide, slavery and cultural destruction. This interpretation emphasises structural injustice over individual stories and links the conquest to contemporary issues of indigenous rights, land ownership and cultural recognition. The debate over what language to use — “discovery,” “encounter,” “invasion,” or “conquest” — is itself a historical argument about perspective and power.

lesson_title: Exam technique and synthesis
content_html:
What This Unit Asks You to Do

The exam for this unit tests four assessment objectives: knowledge and understanding (recall and understanding), analysis of second-order concepts such as cause, consequence and significance (explanation and analysis), evaluation of sources (source analysis) and evaluation of interpretations (interpretation analysis). Each question type targets specific objectives with specific mark allocations. This lesson brings all the skills together, using the voyages and conquest as the content. The key principle is simple: the question tells you which skill to demonstrate. Reading the question carefully is not optional — it is the most important thing you do.

Key Fact

The four assessment objectives are: recall and understanding (knowledge), explanation and analysis (analysis of second-order concepts), source analysis (source evaluation) and interpretation analysis (interpretation evaluation). Extended essays test recall and understanding + explanation and analysis together; source utility questions test source analysis; interpretation comparison and evaluation questions test interpretation analysis

Source Utility: The Three-Lens Approach

The 5-mark source utility question asks you to judge how useful a source is for a specific enquiry. Top-band answers must integrate three things: content (what the source actually says), provenance (who wrote it, when and why) and contextual knowledge (what you know from your studies that helps judge the source’s accuracy or limitations).

A common error is to make a judgement based on provenance alone (“Cortés wrote this to impress the king, so it is biased and therefore useless”). This misses the point: a biased source is still useful — it reveals the author’s perspective, the claims being made, and the political context. The question is: useful for what? A letter by Cortés is highly useful for understanding Spanish justifications for the conquest; it is less useful as a reliable account of what the Aztecs thought. Specify the enquiry the question gives you and judge usefulness for that specific purpose.

Suppose the question is: “How useful is this extract from Bernal Díaz’s Historia Verdadera for an enquiry into the Spanish experience of entering Tenochtitlán?”

Weak response: “This source is useful because it is a first-hand account. However, it may be biased because Díaz was a Spanish soldier. Therefore it is only partially useful.” (This scores low: no content discussed, no contextual knowledge, provenance only one-dimensional.)

Strong response: “The source is useful for understanding the Spanish sense of awe on entering Tenochtitlán because Díaz describes the scale of the markets and canals in detail. The provenance supports its usefulness for this specific enquiry: Díaz was an eyewitness, and unlike Cortés, he had less personal incentive to exaggerate since he was writing a memoir rather than a justification to the king. However, the source was written approximately fifty years after the events, which means Díaz’s memory may have been affected by the subsequent history of the conquest. My knowledge confirms that Tenochtitlán had a population of approximately 200,000–300,000, which supports his impression of a vast and impressive city.”

Interpretation Questions: Why, Not What

The 10-mark compare interpretations question is one of the most commonly mishandled question types. Students who describe what each interpretation says — “Interpretation A says the conquest was driven by greed; Interpretation B says it was driven by religion” — are answering a different question. The marks are for explaining WHY the interpretations differ.

A strong compare-interpretations answer explains: the authors’ identities and backgrounds (a sixteenth-century Spanish friar vs a twenty-first-century decolonial historian); the purpose of each account (reform from within vs challenge to the legacy of colonialism); the evidence each author had available (contemporary Spanish sources only vs modern access to codices and Nahua testimony); and the time in which they wrote (within the colonial period vs in a postcolonial academic context).

Key Fact

To explain why interpretations differ, address: (1) Author’s background (soldier, friar, modern historian); (2) Purpose (justify, criticise, commemorate, academic analysis); (3) Evidence available (contemporary sources only vs modern scholarship); (4) Time of writing (during conquest vs postcolonial era).

Extended Essay Technique

The 12-mark and 16-mark extended responses test your ability to make a substantiated overall judgement. The most common weakness examiners identify is a response that describes two factors or two sides without reaching a conclusion. Describing is not evaluating. You must weigh the evidence and make a supported decision.

A workable framework for 12-mark interpretation essays and 16-mark period essays is four paragraphs:

Paragraph 1: Agree with the interpretation (or support the stated view). Give your strongest evidence. Explain why it supports the interpretation, not just what it is.

Paragraph 2: Disagree or complicate the interpretation. Give evidence that challenges or qualifies it. Again, explain the link to the question explicitly.

Paragraph 3 (for 16-mark): A second supporting point or a more developed counter-argument, depending on the question.

Conclusion: Reach a substantiated overall judgement. Avoid “on one hand, on the other hand, overall I think both sides are important.” Instead: “The interpretation is largely supported by the evidence because [reason], although [counter-evidence] means it is not the whole picture.” Use the word “because” in your conclusion — it forces you to justify the judgement.

Synthesis: Connecting the Unit

Extended essay questions may ask you to connect different parts of the unit. For example: “How far was indigenous opposition the main reason the Spanish conquest of Mexico took three years (1519–1521)?” Here you need to bring together material from different lessons: Cortés’s strategic decisions, indigenous alliances, the Cholula massacre, La Noche Triste, the smallpox epidemic and the siege of Tenochtitlán. The skill is selecting the most relevant evidence and organising it to answer the specific question, not listing everything you know. Synthesis means choosing the right tools from your knowledge toolkit — not emptying the entire toolkit onto the page.
